messages.subject: Re: Tidal currents and distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tiago and list,
Many thanks for your very useful response and sorry for taking so long =
to
reply.... Christmas and all that. I found particularly useful in your
response the concrete identification of the violation of the assumption =
of
non random movement relative to the observer as a mechanism whereby =
tidal
currents could cause problems for distance sampling. Previously, I could =
see
that tidal currents could potentially cause problems but had not =
identified
clearly which underlying assumptions might be violated.=20

The development area covers an area of c. 13 km sq, with linear =
dimensions
of c. 6 km x 2 km. The proposed study area covers an area of c. 85 km =
sq.,
providing a buffer of 4 km around the development area along the =
direction
of the principal tidal currents, and 2 km around the development
perpendicular to this direction. The intention is to cover the whole =
study
area at 1-2 monthly intervals over the year (taking c. 1-2 days) with
additional more detailed small scale surveys in the immediate vicinity =
of
the development area to characterize variation with different states of =
the
tide. However, although there are obviously  issues with respect to the
appropriate spatial scale and frequency of surveys my principal concerns =
at
the moment are how in strong tidal regimes do we design line transect
surveys and analyse the data so as to obtain unbiased/accurate estimates =
of
density, and how do we interpret these density estimates -as =
straightforward
density estimates or flow rates.

The strength of tidal currents in this area are such that at many states =
of
the tide it would be impossible to go against the flow, and so the =
design
axis has been chosen so that transects run roughly perpendicular to the
principal direction of the currents. Indeed the strength of the currents =
is
so strong that we have had to use a variation (see below) of the even =
spaced
zigzag transect design rather than the systematic parallel transect =
design
we might have favoured, as sailing completely perpendicular to the =
currents
is also likely to be impossible at some stages of the tide. Our =
variation on
the zigzag design is to provide an offset between subsequent transects =
to
prevent overlap of coverage, otherwise given the small spatial scale of =
the
study area relative to transect spacing/width, subsequent transects =
would
have been overlapping for c.30% of their length. Dropping coverage from =
one
transect for overlapping areas would thus have significantly reduced =
effort;
we were also concerned that dropping coverage of overlapping areas from =
one
transect would bias coverage toward the centre of the study area. With =
this
"trapezium" design, if the width of the offset design is set to zero, =
the
equal spaced zigzag design is recovered, if it is set to the same as the
transect spacing, the systematic parallel transect design is recovered. =
We
are currently evaluating its  coverage properties.=20

For the practical reasons given above our current design is based upon
transects running roughly perpendicular to the tidal current rather than
parallel.  However, setting practical issues aside, I also wonder if =
having
transects running parallel to the current could cause statistical =
problems.
For example, if birds are moving with the current, and your moving in =
the
same direction, then if you start a transect on a water column  holding
relatively low numbers of birds, then you will tend to underestimate
densities for that transect. Conversely, if you start the transect on a
water column holding relatively high numbers of birds you will tend to
overestimate densities.  On the other hand When heading upstream, you =
will
tend to record many more birds than when heading downstream, of compared =
to
being stationary. I'm not sure what the statistical consequences of =
that,
but can see that unless (for example) you take into account current =
speeds,
the densities on transects heading upstream are likely to be =
overestimated,
and the variance in encounter rates between transects is likely to be =
much
greater than if transects are perpendicular to the current.=20

Given the above, and the fact that this is an applied rather than pure
project my current intention is to use (simple) simulation modeling to
explore the potential biases in such data, and suggest appropriate
correction factors. However, given the time limited/applied nature of =
the
project I don't think aiming for a full analytical solution (providing
confidence limits etc.) is likely to be possible.=20

However, before embarking on this path, just wanted to make sure I =
wasn't
reinventing the wheel, nor miss opportunities for possible cooperation =
if
others are encountering similar problems.=20

Once again, any response gratefully received.

Best wishes

Nigel

Nigel Harding

-----Original Message-----
From: Wildlife abundance estimation using distance sampling techniques.
[mailto:DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK] On Behalf Of Tiago Marques
Sent: 21 December 2011 01:25
To: DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK
Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] Tidal currents and distance sampling

Dear Nigel, list,

Your study seems quite interesting, but I'm not sure you provide all the =

required information to answer the questions you ask. The best way to=20
address the problem will depend strongly on what are the purposes of=20
inference, namely at what spatial and temporal scale do you require=20
density estimates, as well as how serious/persistent the tidal currents =
are.

 From the distance sampling perspective, if what you have is a line=20
transect and the tidal current is perpendicular to it, one of the=20
fundamental conventional distance sampling assumptions is violated: you=20
have non-random movement, as animals are coming towards you; if their=20
speed is negligible to boat speed, you might ignore it, but otherwise=20
you run into trouble and will tend to overestimate abundance. In that=20
sense, it might better to attempt to have the transect parallel to the=20
current, but then other issues might pop up (e.g. if there's some animal =

density gradient with respect to the lines).

I hope this helps.

Cheers,

Tiago

On 20/12/2011 17:15, Nigel Harding wrote:
> > Dear all,
> >
> > I am currently planning boat based surveys in support of the EIA =
process
for
> > a tidal energy device, and I'm beginning to think about the =
interpretation
> > of the data. I can see that strong tidal currents might have important
> > consequences for both the accuracy of density estimates (e.g. with a =
tidal
> > current perpendicular to the transect additional birds "flowing" into =
the
> > transect from the side) and their interpretation (e.g. birds/m2 or
> > birds/m2/second) and that these consequences will depend critically =
upon
> > whether birds are holding their position against the current, or =
flowing
> > with it, or some position in between.
> >
> >
> >
> > Is this a problem other people have encountered or are encountering, =
and
> > there is guidance available on how deal with this situation, including
what
> > needs recording in the field (e.g. water speed as well as ground =
speed).
> >

messages.subject: MRDS-Strata as replicates
messages.body_plain:
Hello list,

I'm analyzing a narwhal aerial survey for which I have 6 strata, one of w=
hich was flown twice. We used standard MRDS sampling techniques (2 isolat=
ed observers on either side of the plane) and I'm analyzing the data usin=
g the MRDS analysis engine in Distance. Due to the low density of animals=
, we have only 147 groups in the analysis, after 6 days of surveys.  So, =
I am using all of the observations to calculate one detection function wh=
ich I then use to calculate abundances by stratum. To calculate the total=
 abundance, I am summing the per stratum estimates.=20

My question is this: for the one stratum that was surveyed twice, I want =
to calculate an effort weighted mean. A concern that has been brought up =
in the past is that, since I am using the same detection curve for the tw=

messages.subject: manipulating Effective Strip Width (ESW) values for site-to-site
messages.subject_clean: manipulating Effective Strip Width (ESW) values for site-to-site
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

     I have completed initial Distance analysis of transect data for
primates and large frugivorous birds from three tropical forest sites
in Peru.  My survey effort at each site was just over 100km, and the
analysis was done on a site-by-site basis, with no pooling or
stratification (as I am looking to compare densities across sites).
As such, the data is a bit sparse for a few species, but nonetheless
exhibits useful trends.  My main concern - likely a result of the
limited quantity of data - is that several values for Effective Strip
Width (ESW) generated by Distance (using the Hazard Rate Simple
Polynomial model with R truncation of 5% and L truncation of 1m) are
either lower or higher than expected.  The final density estimates
reflect this, and I believe could be improved given a more accurate
estimate of ESW.  Variability in ESW values across sites but for the
same species is especially concerning, given that the true ESW values
should be consistent; as all three forest sites have the same basic
composition and forest structure, a given species should be equally
detectable across them all, and thus ideally would have the same ESW
value for all three sites.
     I could estimate ESW for each species based on my observations of
their detectability, but I am not sure whether it would be acceptable
or even possible to input these estimated ESW values manually, which
would also alter the final density value.  If it is possible and
acceptable to directly manipulate the ESW, how can I do that?  If it
is not, is there another approach that I could take which would
otherwise increase or decrease a given ESW value (and consequently the
density estimate as well) to a level that I feel is appropriate, and
consistent across the three sites?
     I appreciate any advice or suggestions you might have.  If you
have questions in response to my post, I would be happy to elaborate.
Thanks very much for your time!!  Sincerely,

Cooper Rosin
cooper...@duke.edu
Masters of Environmental Management Candidate
Duke University

messages.body_plain:
Hi Cooper,

ESW is just the strip width multiplied by the estimated detection
probability, so if you have a lot of variation in ESW it is probably
because your estimated detection functions vary considerably.  If there is
no reason to suspect that the true detection function varies between sites,
then the question is why your estimated detection functions vary so much.
 I'm guessing its because of small sample sizes.  Again, if there is no
reason to suspect that the true detection function varies between
sites, then perhaps you should consider pooling detections across sites to
estimate your detection function. You can still get site-specific density
estimates.

Cheers,

--

messages.subject_clean: generating robust estimates for rare species (hunted vs.
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

     I have a follow-up question to one I posed earlier.  I completed
a transect study of primates and large frugivorous birds across three
tropical forest sites in Peru.  The sites are under varying degrees of
hunting pressure, with one intact site, one moderate site, and one
highly impacted site.  My survey effort at each site was just over
100km, and the Distance analysis was done on a site-by-site basis,
with no pooling or stratification.  Given that some of my target
species occur at very low densities as a result of hunting pressures,
the data and resulting Distance analysis is not very robust.  I have a
few questions in response to this:

1.  How does one generate a robust density estimate for a species
which is so rarely encountered?  My understanding is that pooling the
data for a given species across all three sites would be inappropriate
in this case, as the detectability of that species is not the same
across sites (the animals at a hunted site will respond by avoiding
surveyors and fleeing more quickly and quietly, thus they will be less
detectable than at an intact site, which will skew the estimates).

2.  It seems that generating a good density estimate of a rarely
encountered species would require an astronomical amount of survey
effort.  Is there a consensus guideline for the minimum recommended
effort?  I have read that 40 observations is a good general minimum,
but that is an unreasonable goal for a rare species...

3.  If after 10 weeks of intensive field study, I am not able to
generate enough data for a robust density estimate of a rarely
encountered species, how useful is Distance as a conservation tool for
assessing populations of rare species?

     I have read through the Distance Sampling book and several
additional publications guiding the sampling of tropical forest
primates, but I am not able to find specific answers to these
questions.  I would appreciate any feedback or suggestions on how to
proceed with my analysis.  If you have questions in response to my
post, I would be happy to elaborate. If this is a recurring question
among the Distance community, I would gladly compile the responses to
this post to share.  Thanks very much for your time!!  Sincerely,

Cooper Rosin
cooper...@duke.edu
Masters of Environmental Management Candidate
Duke University

messages.body_plain:
A hammer is not always the right tool for the job. Likewise, distance
sampling will not work for every situation! You can always pool data
across site and species that have similar detectability as was suggested
in a previous post.  But if that is not what you want to do you may need
a different approach. Analyzing as a strip transect simply ignores the
detectability issue and is not a good solution.  For rare species that
are uniquely identifiable, I would recommend capture-recapture using
photo-identification.

--jeff
